blocks.text: “Don’t you dare,” I screamed, and the force of my own voice seemed to tear through the roar of the creek.
I could not know whether he heard the words.
I wrapped the rope around the trunk again, taking the strain off my hands, and looked toward the mule standing a few yards away with its lead trailing in the mud.
All my life, people had looked at my size and decided it was the most important thing about me.
For once, I was grateful for every inch.
I dragged myself to the lead, caught it, and brought the gray mule beside the tree.
The animal shook, but she knew the pressure of a rope and the voice of a frightened person trying not to sound frightened.
I used the free length Magnus had carried back across the bridge, fastening it to the strained line where I could reach.
I made the second with the stubborn concentration of a woman mending a garment she could not afford to lose.
Then I brought the line across the stout part of the pack saddle.
Magnus’s shoulder came clear of the trapped branches.
He caught the sloping bank with one hand.
I shouted at the mule until my voice broke.
He rose through the brown water as though the mountain were unwillingly returning something it had meant to keep.
When his chest reached the mud, I crawled toward him.
I caught the collar of his coat with both hands.
Together, with the mule’s weight holding the line, we brought him far enough onto the bank that the creek could no longer reach his face.
I lay beside him with my cheek against the earth and my leg burning so fiercely that I thought I might faint.
We remained there only long enough for him to breathe properly.
Cold was settling into his clothes, and my strength had become something I could measure in single movements.
He helped me back into the saddle with a care that cost him visibly.
The second mule remained across the broken creek.
Magnus looked back once, then tied her loose enough to reach shelter and feed until someone could return by the longer trail.
We carried nothing we could not do without.
Magnus walked with one hand on the saddle, using the mule’s movement to steady his bruised leg.
I kept my eyes open because he asked me to.
At first, I thought the yellow window was another fever dream.
Then Hyram opened the door and came down the steps with a lantern.
His face changed when the light reached us.
It was the only word he managed before his knees bent.
I remember a room that smelled of coffee and damp wool.
I remember someone putting more wood in a stove while Magnus argued that he could remain standing.
Then the doctor came from the settlement below, brought by a rider Hyram sent before the lantern was cold.
What followed was painful, humiliating, and blessedly ordinary.
There was light held by someone whose hands were not shaking from exhaustion.
There was a doctor who examined the wound, found a small splinter Magnus had been unable to see, and spoke without pretending that recovery would be quick.
The wood had passed through flesh outside the joint.
Magnus sat beside the bed with a blanket around his shoulders and his damaged hand covering his mouth.
Later, when the doctor had gone downstairs and the room finally became quiet, I asked him why he had reached for his knife in the creek.
“I thought you’d try to hold me with your hands.”
“No,” he said, “I keep forgetting someone might choose the trouble of saving me.”
That was the earned truth beneath everything he had done.
He had never learned how to become one without shame.
My strength returned in humiliating little pieces, first sitting without dizziness, then standing, then crossing the room with Magnus beside me and a walking stick beneath my hand.
He sent for the second mule, replaced what he could from my lost trunk, and brought my mother’s comb back after Hyram’s men found the battered chest lodged beneath fallen branches.
One afternoon, when I could walk to the station porch, Magnus found me watching the road.
He was keeping the promise he had made beside the bed.
I stepped close enough that he had to lift his eyes the smallest amount to meet mine.
We married when I could stand through the vows without leaning on anything except his hand.
By spring, the shelter was rebuilt, the trail repaired, and a second hook hung beside the door at precisely the height I preferred.
Sometimes, when he thought I was not looking, he watched me move through the cabin with an expression I had once believed no man would wear for me.
“Nothing,” I said the first evening we sat together at the table, our knees touching beneath the boards he had made room for me to use.
Then I took his scarred hand in mine and corrected myself.
